name: Chlortalidone

card.summary: A long-acting thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic; a possible water pill in forum lists, with no appearance data.
card.note: Prescription-only; can lower potassium and sodium and raise blood sugar.

quick.overview:
Chlortalidone (also spelled chlorthalidone) is a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic and a first-line treatment for high blood pressure. It has been in medical use since 1960.

It is included in this wiki as a diuretic sometimes grouped with water pills. No study has examined it for puffiness or any appearance goal.
quick.mechanism: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule and also inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Its half-life of about 40 hours is longer than that of hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
quick.risks: Reported effects include low potassium and sodium, high blood sugar, dizziness, erectile dysfunction, high uric acid and photosensitivity. It is prescription-only and banned in some sports.[1]

lead: Chlortalidone (also spelled chlorthalidone) is an oral thiazide-like diuretic, a prescription medicine used as a first-line treatment for hypertension and for edema caused by heart, liver or kidney disease. It is also used for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and preventing calcium kidney stones.[1]

In appearance and physique communities it is mentioned as a 'water pill': by increasing the excretion of sodium and water it reduces fluid retention, and people interested in a leaner or less puffy look have discussed diuretics of this kind in that context. The chain people describe runs from more sodium and water in the urine, to less extracellular fluid, to a drier, more defined look. Forum posters in bodybuilding spaces also mention it in connection with blood-pressure control and with lists of drugs banned by testing bodies.[5][6][7] No published research has tested chlortalidone for facial depuffing, leanness or other cosmetic uses.

It was patented in 1957 and entered medical use in 1960, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1][2] It is slowly absorbed and has a half-life of around 40 hours, which Wikipedia says may help explain its greater blood-pressure effect compared with hydrochlorothiazide.[1] Its main body of research comprises large cardiovascular outcome trials such as ALLHAT and the Diuretic Comparison Project, which together enrolled tens of thousands of people.[10][11]

chain: Blocks sodium-chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule
More sodium and water leave in urine
Less fluid retention, which users associate with a leaner, less puffy look
angle.text: Chlortalidone increases urinary excretion of sodium and water, and users in physique circles discuss diuretics as a way to reduce fluid retention. This use is claimed rather than studied; clinical research examines blood pressure and edema, not cosmetic outcomes.[1][5]

infobox: Onset within about 3 hours; effects can last up to 3 days[1]
Prescription-only; on lists of banned diuretics in some sports[1]
Generic; 124th most prescribed US drug in 2023[1]

paras: Chlortalidone treats hypertension, edema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and calcium oxalate stone recurrence. Wikipedia reports it reduces left ventricular mass, that a secondary analysis of ALLHAT data suggested it may help prevent hip and pelvic fractures, and that evidence for Meniere disease is limited to small, low-quality studies.[1] Product labelling sets dosing for each use, and Grokipedia summarises it.[2]

Diuretics reduce extracellular fluid, and bodybuilding forums have long discussed them in connection with contest conditioning, which is why chlortalidone appears on banned-substance lists posted there.[7][9] One 2024 T Nation poster who takes chlorthalidone for blood pressure and heart disease wrote that it is a 'water tablet' and that he was told it is not permitted for competition.[6]

Wikipedia's article on diuretics describes sports uses as rapid weight loss to make a weight class, in sports such as boxing and wrestling, and as a way to dilute urine and mask other drugs in testing; it mentions no cosmetic uses.[17]

Wikipedia states a meta-analysis found greater blood-pressure reduction than hydrochlorothiazide with similar side effects, and that low doses worked about as well as higher ones in ALLHAT.[1] A 2019 meta-analysis summarised by Grokipedia reports about 3.3 mmHg greater systolic reduction than hydrochlorothiazide.[2] Reviews disagree on whether its risks match or exceed those of hydrochlorothiazide, with some reporting more hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.[1][8]

Head-to-head outcome data are discussed in the clinical studies section: the largest randomized comparison with hydrochlorothiazide found similar cardiovascular event rates, while the CLICK trial found a large blood-pressure effect in advanced kidney disease.[11][13]

Common effects include low potassium and sodium, high blood sugar, dizziness and erectile dysfunction; others include low magnesium, high calcium and uric acid, gout (risk roughly doubled), photosensitivity and pancreatitis. One review found low magnesium in about 20 percent of patients taking 50 mg daily, and hyponatremia was more common in older adults. It is considered a less preferred option in pregnancy, crosses the placenta and enters breast milk.[1]

Chlortalidone inhibits the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, reducing sodium and chloride reabsorption. Unlike classic thiazides it also strongly inhibits several carbonic anhydrase isoforms, which may contribute to its diuretic effect, and the mechanism of its long-term blood-pressure lowering is not fully understood.[1]

It is absorbed slowly, is about 75 percent protein-bound, has a half-life of about 40 hours and is excreted mostly unchanged by the kidneys, so reduced kidney function prolongs it. Wikipedia suggests the long duration explains why it stays effective if doses are missed.[1] Chemically it is a sulfamoylbenzamide (C14H11ClN2O4S) lacking the benzothiadiazine ring of classic thiazides, hence 'thiazide-like'.[1]

The Diuretic Wikipedia article describes the broader class mechanism: thiazides block the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, water follows sodium into the urine, the short-term pressure effect comes from reduced preload, and the long-term effect is attributed to a vasodilator action that is not fully explained.[17]

Chlortalidone was patented in 1957 and entered medical use in 1960; Wikipedia's categories list it among drugs developed by Novartis, and trade names include Hygroton and Thalitone, with a Hemiclor tablet also cited.[1] It later became a standard comparator in hypertension research. The ALLHAT trial, which ran from 1994 to 2002, used it as the reference first-step drug against amlodipine and lisinopril, and its results fed into guidelines that place thiazide-type diuretics among first-line agents.[10][16] The 2022 Diuretic Comparison Project extended that line of research to a head-to-head contest with the more widely prescribed hydrochlorothiazide.[11]

The drug is banned in some sports because diuretics aid weight-class cutting and can mask other substances in urine tests; forum users repost banned lists naming chlorthalidone among prescription diuretics.[1][7][9] In 2023 it was the 124th most commonly prescribed drug in the US, with over 5 million prescriptions, and the FDA announced a recall of over 11,000 bottles of 25 mg tablets from one manufacturer for failed dissolution specifications.[1]

Wikipedia notes it is prescription-only in the UK and US, available as a generic, and banned in some sports including cricket because diuretics can reduce body weight for weight-class sports or mask other drugs in urine tests.[1] Doping-control laboratories developed multi-diuretic screening methods for this reason.[18]

ALLHAT, a randomized double-blind trial run from 1994 to 2002 at 623 North American centers, enrolled 33,357 people aged 55 or older with hypertension and another coronary risk factor and assigned them to chlorthalidone 12.5 to 25 mg per day (15,255 people), amlodipine (9,048) or lisinopril (9,054) for 4 to 8 years; the primary outcome was fatal coronary heart disease or nonfatal myocardial infarction.[10] Six-year primary outcome rates were 11.5% with chlorthalidone, 11.3% with amlodipine and 11.4% with lisinopril, with no meaningful difference. Heart failure was higher with amlodipine (10.2% vs 7.7%) and lisinopril (8.7% vs 7.7%), and stroke was higher with lisinopril (6.3% vs 5.6%). The investigators concluded that thiazide-type diuretics were superior at preventing one or more forms of cardiovascular disease and recommended them as preferred first-step therapy.[10]

The Diuretic Comparison Project, a pragmatic trial in the US Department of Veterans Affairs, randomized 13,523 adults aged 65 or older who were taking hydrochlorothiazide to continue it or switch to chlorthalidone, with median follow-up of 2.4 years. The composite primary outcome occurred in 10.4% of the chlorthalidone group and 10.0% of the hydrochlorothiazide group (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.16), and hypokalemia was more common with chlorthalidone (6.0% vs 4.4%).[11] A secondary analysis examined kidney outcomes.[12]

The CLICK trial randomized 160 people with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and poorly controlled hypertension to chlorthalidone or placebo. At 12 weeks the 24-hour systolic pressure fell by 11.0 mm Hg with chlorthalidone versus 0.5 mm Hg with placebo, a difference of 10.5 mm Hg; hypokalemia, reversible creatinine rises, hyperglycemia, dizziness and hyperuricemia were more frequent with chlorthalidone.[13] A randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial of 113 postmenopausal women with systolic hypertension, with a mean 2.6 years of chlorthalidone use, reported lower annual bone loss than placebo at the sites measured.[14]

Registered trials include a 940-participant comparison of treatment regimens, an azilsartan plus chlorthalidone combination study in 551 participants and another in 1,711 participants with moderate to severe hypertension.[3][4][19] No studies have examined chlortalidone for facial depuffing or other appearance goals.

timeline.event: ALLHAT begins enrolment; ends 2002 with 33,357 participants.[10]
CLICK trial in advanced chronic kidney disease published.[13]
Diuretic Comparison Project compares chlorthalidone with hydrochlorothiazide in veterans.[11]

lore.intro: Chlortalidone appears on T Nation mostly in blood-pressure discussions and in reposted banned-substance lists rather than as a stand-alone appearance tool.[5][6][7][9]

claims.claim: A small dose of chlorthalidone is a reasonable thing for strength athletes to use.
claims.believers: A 2005 forum poster asked why a small dose should be a bad idea when athletes take other supplements to raise muscle mass, adding that elevated blood pressure is rare in athletes.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes chlortalidone is banned in some sports and carries risks including low potassium and sodium.[1]

claims.claim: As a water tablet it can help physique conditioning for contests.
claims.believers: Posters note it is a 'water tablet' and one was told it is not permitted for competition.[6]
claims.experts: Governing bodies list diuretics as banned because they can reduce weight and mask other drugs.[1]

claims.claim: Chlorthalidone is a normal choice for lowering blood pressure in lifters.
claims.believers: A 2010 poster suggested chlorthalidone or amlodipine as options to use while other methods bring blood pressure into range.[15]
claims.experts: Guidelines and reviews list thiazide-like diuretics as first-line antihypertensives.[1][16]
